messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 44

He is a 35-year-old Latin American man who makes his living as a musician, and before the accident he thinks of himself as someone who lives by rhythm, movement, and improvisation. His days are built around rehearsals, late-night gigs, loading equipment, and the easy, familiar chaos of the music world. He is married, and he and his wife have a life that feels ordinary in the best way: shared meals, talk about bills and schedules, arguments about small things, plans for the future. He does not imagine that this steadiness can be taken apart in a few seconds.

The accident happens abruptly, without warning, on a day that begins like many others. He is driving between commitments when everything changes in an instant. He remembers metal, noise, a violent jolt, and then the strange suspension of time that comes after impact. For a moment he cannot tell whether he is alive. He becomes aware of pain, then of panic rising in his chest, then of the realization that he cannot control what is happening to his body or the scene around him. The memory remains fragmented for him, held in flashes rather than a full sequence, but certain details stay sharp: the smell, the sound, the helplessness, the conviction that he may die there.

In the days afterward, he moves through the world as if it has narrowed. He is physically shaken and repeatedly surprised by how afraid he feels even when he is safe. He begins to scan for danger automatically, especially in traffic. When he hears screeching brakes or a sudden bang, his body reacts before his mind can catch up. His heart pounds, his muscles tighten, and for a second he is back in the crash, disoriented and bracing for impact. He hates how quickly it happens and how little control he has over it. As a musician, he is used to listening closely, to noticing changes in tempo or mood, but now his nervous system seems tuned only to threat.

He starts avoiding anything that reminds him of the accident. At first it is driving the route where it happened, then driving at all unless he absolutely must. He asks his wife to take over errands. He lets phone calls go to voicemail if they come while he is in the car. He notices that he is less spontaneous, more rigid, planning each day around how to reduce the chance of being startled. Even music, the thing that has always felt like home, becomes complicated. The sound of certain low frequencies or sudden percussion can hit him like a physical blow. In rehearsals he sits a little more tensely than before, watching exits, finding it harder to settle into the flow he used to trust.

At night, he does not sleep deeply. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes from dreams that leave him sweating and confused. Sometimes the dreams replay the accident in distorted pieces; other times there is only the feeling of being trapped, of having to escape something he cannot see. He wakes with his jaw clenched and his body ready to move. On the worst mornings he lies still for a few minutes, trying to convince himself that he is in his bedroom and not in the wreck. His wife notices that he is more irritable and less patient, especially when he is tired. He feels ashamed of snapping at her, then withdraws from conversation because he does not know how to explain that he is constantly on edge.

He also becomes more distant from the version of himself that once felt easygoing and open. He remembers laughing more, talking more freely after shows, feeling connected to other musicians. Now he often feels cut off, as if there is a glass wall between him and everyone else. He is not sure how much to say when people ask how he is doing, so he gives the safe answer and changes the subject. Part of him fears that if he starts talking about the accident, he will flood with feeling and lose control. Another part fears that nothing will change anyway, that the event has already altered him in a permanent way. He grieves the loss of his old confidence and the simple trust he used to have in ordinary days.

Over time, he returns to work in pieces, but he is not unchanged. He can still perform, and there are moments when music gives him brief relief, a place where his attention gathers and the world feels coherent again. Yet even on stage he is aware of his body, of noises in the crowd, of the possibility that something could go wrong. He is working hard to keep moving, to remain a husband, a performer, and himself, while carrying the accident with him in ways he did not choose.
